title: How To Handle Students Who Don’t Do Any Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses students who refuse to do any work, arguing that common accommodating strategies — coddling, bribing, and one-on-one hand-holding — actually deepen resistance and undercut the development of a genuine work ethic. He proposes three steps instead: deliver exceptionally clear, compelling whole-class instruction so students know exactly what to do; then step back and let students face the real choice to work or not, without rescuing them; and finally, when students do produce work, praise the content of that work specifically rather than praising them for merely trying. He acknowledges this approach can feel harsh at first but argues it is the only route to authentic improvement and a true, earned sense of accomplishment.
points: Argues that coddling, bribing, and constant one-on-one help for reluctant workers enables their inaction and undermines their long-term motivation.
Step one is to teach exceptionally clear, engaging whole-class lessons that thoroughly set students up to work independently.
Step two is to 'let them be' — resisting the urge to kneel down and rescue students who initially sit and do nothing.
Step three is to praise the work itself, quickly and specifically, rather than praising the student for effort or trying.
Frames withholding rescue as compassionate, arguing that facing the real choice to work or fail is what ultimately motivates change.
quotes: You see, by spending extra time with reluctant students, by coddling, appeasing, and buying into any of an unlimited number of justifications for their inaction, you create even more resistance.

Meanwhile, these same students who are assumed to be too attentive-averse or ill-equipped to succeed rush home at the end of another wasted day and play the same video game for three hours without a break.
You must be able to draw them in, absorb them in the moment, and maintain their state of flow— where time slows, mind-energy focuses, and concerns and worries of the past and future fade away.
Forcing their hand is the change-agent they desperately need to upend their downward trajectory.

Instead of rushing over with a huge smile and telling the student how wonderful they are because they completed a few sentences—which very effectively lowers the bar of expectation—point out their good work.
In the meantime, they’re a living and breathing reminder for you to be better.
